newsitem.title: CHINA: China leaps to defence of Hong Kong newspaper.
newsitem.headline: China leaps to defence of Hong Kong newspaper.

text.p: Beijing's English-language mouthpiece, the China Daily, on Thursday leapt to the defence of a Hong Kong newspaper accused of taking undue note of mainland opinion in the run-up to the end of British colonial rule.

The appointment of a former China Daily editor as consultant to the South China Morning Post had been twisted by Western media to suggest censorship was being imposed in Hong Kong ahead of its July 1 return to Beijing rule, the newspaper said.

China had guaranteed that Hong Kong's way of life would not change for 50 years after the midnight handover, while South China Morning Post Editor Jonathan Fenby had made clear the new consultant would do no more than consult, it said.
"British and American correspondents have jumped at the opportunity to prosecute China for the newspaper's decision," it said in a ringing denunciation of Western journalism.
"Should not these people feed more facts and fewer fears to their readers and viewers?" it asked. "What is their job? To inform or misinform the general public?"

Many journalists and residents in Hong Kong fear that self-censorship is growing more common among the free-wheeling territory's independent press ahead of the return to China, where newspapers and broadcasters are strictly controlled.
Chinese courts have in recent years jailed both mainland and Hong Kong journalists for reporting what in the West would be considered routine economic information.
China Daily quoted Post editor Fenby himself as condemning the Western media for being sometimes "malevolent and contemptuous of reality".

Foreign news providers were paying too little attention to the 1839 anti-narcotics campaign of Qing dynasty (1644-1911) official Lin Zexu, whose seizure of foreign opium stocks led to the Opium War and the seizure of Hong Kong by Britain, it said.
"Does any mention of this man get printed in the Western press?" it asked.
